lesson.title: The Default Route: The Router's Answer for Everything Else
lesson.summary: A default route is a catch all routing table entry that matches any destination not covered by a more specific route, typically used to send traffic toward a single gateway out of a network.
lesson.body:
A routing table cannot realistically hold an entry for every network that exists on the internet, there are far too many, and most of them are irrelevant to any single router most of the time. Instead, routers rely on a special entry called the default route, conventionally written as the prefix 0.0.0.0/0, which matches every possible destination address. Because of longest prefix match, this entry is only used when nothing more specific matches: any route to a smaller, more precise prefix will always win, and the default route quietly catches whatever is left over.

This pattern shows up constantly at the edge of networks. A home router typically knows about exactly one specific network, the devices on your home Wi-Fi, and for literally everything else, every website, every server, anything not on that local network, it has a single default route pointing at the internet service provider's router. That one entry stands in for the millions of destinations the home router will never individually learn about. The same idea scales up: a mid sized company network might have specific routes to its own branch offices and a default route pointing toward its internet provider for everything beyond that.

Default routes are very often configured as static routes, since the whole point is usually a single, stable, obvious path out of a stub network, but they do not have to be, dynamic routing protocols can also learn and advertise a default route on a network's behalf. Either way, the underlying mechanism is the same one governing every routing table lookup: when a packet arrives for a destination with no matching specific entry, the router falls back to whatever route matches the least, the default, rather than dropping the packet outright.
